assumptions: The incoming particles have identical positive rest mass m0 and the target is initially stationary.

solutions.method: Treat the other two decay products as one recoil system and minimize its invariant mass.
assumptions: The parent is initially at rest with positive mass m0; no products other than the three specified particles carry energy or momentum.
The decay is kinematically allowed only if m0≥m1+m2+m3. All masses are nonnegative; the common-velocity construction directly attains the maximum for positive recoil masses.
The maximum is a kinematic bound. Decay matrix elements or selection rules may suppress events at the endpoint.

steps.explanation: Let the pair of particles 2 and 3 have total four-momentum Q. Conservation makes it recoil opposite particle 1.
Define the recoil-pair invariant mass M23 and eliminate particle 1 momentum using its mass shell.
The pair energy in its own centre-of-inertia frame is at least its summed rest energy. For positive masses this minimum occurs when particles 2 and 3 have zero relative velocity.
At the endpoint the recoiling pair and particle 1 obey ordinary two-body kinematics; the expression is feasible precisely above the three-body threshold.

answers.notes: Requires m0≥m1+m2+m3. For positive masses, daughters 2 and 3 have a common velocity at this endpoint.

checks: At threshold m0=m1+m2+m3 the formula gives E1,max=m1c² and all three daughters can be at rest.
The expression is symmetric under exchange of daughters 2 and 3, as required.
If the recoil pair is massless, its minimum invariant mass is zero when its members are collinear; the formula then reduces to the corresponding two-body endpoint.
limitations: For a recoil pair containing one massive and one massless daughter, the minimum pair mass is approached as the massless particle energy tends to zero. The displayed maximum can then be a supremum at a phase-space boundary rather than an event with all daughter energies nonzero.
If m0 is less than the sum of daughter masses, the proposed decay is forbidden and no physical maximum exists.

solutions.method: Conserve energy and momentum for an infinitesimal exhaust emission in the instantaneous rocket rest frame, then integrate rapidity.
assumptions: Use an inertial frame in which the rocket initially rests, v(m0)=0. The jet is collinear and directed backward, with fixed speed u relative to the instantaneous rocket frame.
The rocket is isolated from external forces and emits only the exhaust. m includes the full instantaneous rocket rest mass, including fuel and its internal energy.

An exhaust element has positive rest mass dmu, energy gamma_u dmu c² and backward momentum −gamma_u dmu u in the instantaneous pre-emission rocket frame. A cold mono-speed exhaust is the model; no extra photons or isotropic heat losses are added.
The statement stipulates u≪c. Retaining gamma_u during conservation makes the mass-energy bookkeeping consistent; the resulting ideal collinear formula also holds for constant exhaust speeds below c.

steps.explanation: Introduce rapidity theta so that infinitesimal boosts add, and describe a single emission in the initially comoving frame.
Conservation of energy to first order includes the rest-frame kinetic energy of the emitted element. The rocket recoil energy is second order in the infinitesimal emission.
Conservation of longitudinal momentum relates the rocket rapidity increment to the exhaust momentum.
Integrate from initial mass m0 and zero rapidity. Convert rapidity to the laboratory velocity.
An equivalent mass-ratio expression and the Newtonian limit make the result transparent.

answers.label: Rocket speed as a function of its remaining rest mass
Rest mass of an infinitesimal cold exhaust element
answers.notes: Lost rocket rest mass and exhaust rest mass differ because the exhaust carries kinetic energy. For u≪c they coincide to leading order only.

checks: The formula gives v(m0)=0, increases as mass is spent, and remains strictly below c for every positive m.
For a small logarithmic mass ratio the ordinary Tsiolkovsky formula is recovered.
The differential law dtheta/dln(m0/m)=u/c satisfies both local momentum and energy conservation. Identifying −dm with dmu exactly while keeping finite gamma_u would violate energy conservation.
Even when u≪c, the rocket can become relativistic if ln(m0/m) is of order c/u; expanding tanh in that regime would be invalid.
limitations: A finite dry mass limits the accessible mass ratio and hence the speed.

If extra energy is radiated or the exhaust has a velocity/thermal distribution, u must be replaced by an effective directed momentum-to-energy exhaust speed; the bulk gas speed alone need not determine the answer.
For an initial speed other than zero, add its rapidity: artanh(v/c)=artanh(v_initial/c)+(u/c)ln(m0/m).
